title: Kanaka's window
hookLine: a shepherd poet isn't let into the temple, so he sings from behind the wall
carry: God turns toward the devotee left outside

lines: A SHEPHERD WHO WASN'T LET IN.
cards: Visit the Krishna temple at Udupi today, the one with the image from the ballast clay, and you'll notice something odd. You don't see Krishna face to face through a big open doorway.

You look at him through a small latticed window, nine little openings in a silver frame. And on the outside of the temple wall, on the west side, there's another window with a story attached, and a shrine to a poet.
The story is about a shepherd who wasn't allowed in.

teach.b: His name was Kanakadasa, a poet from the Kuruba community, shepherds, in Karnataka.
He belonged to the Haridasas, the servants of Hari, who took Madhva's teaching out of Sanskrit and into Kannada songs people could sing in the fields.

His teacher, the Madhva scholar Vyasatirtha, is remembered as loving him. But when Kanaka came to Udupi to see Krishna, the temple authorities of the time, the story goes, wouldn't let him in because of his birth.

teach.h: KEPT OUT, HE SANG FROM THE WALL.
teach.b: So he went around to the back, stood outside the west wall, and sang, and sang, to a Krishna he couldn't see.

teach.h: THE IMAGE TURNED TO FACE HIM.
teach.b: Tradition says the wall cracked open, and the image inside turned around to face him. The crack became a window, still called Kanaka's window, and the image, they say, faces west to this day.
Here's the teaching inside the story. The temple kept a gate; God didn't.
In bhakti, God turns toward love, not birth. And the two stay two: Kanaka is still Kanaka, Krishna still Krishna. But the wall becomes a window.
There's a gentler story about him too. His teacher gave each student a banana and said: eat it where no one can see you. Everyone came back having eaten theirs in some hidden corner.

teach.h: GOD TURNS TOWARD THE DEVOTEE LEFT OUTSIDE.
teach.b: Kanaka came back with his uneaten. Wherever I went, he said, Krishna was watching. Two, always, and never out of sight.
Pilgrims still stop at Kanaka's window, and his own songs ask what birth has to do with God.

how: At the Udupi Krishna temple, devotees view Krishna through a small latticed window, and Kanaka's window on the west wall is honored as a place of pilgrimage; the Haridasa songs of Kanakadasa and Purandaradasa are sung across Karnataka and in Carnatic music.

o: the temple's main gate, opened for all
a song Kanaka sang outside the temple wall
the window where Krishna turned to face Kanaka

s: Kanakadasa was welcomed into the Udupi temple
the story says he was kept out because of his birth, and sang from outside the west wall.
they sang in Kannada, so ordinary people could sing along.
tradition says the Udupi image turned to face Kanaka
the wall cracked, and the crack became Kanaka's window.

games.q: you're Kanakadasa. you've walked to Udupi to see Krishna, and you're refused entry at the temple because of your birth. what does the story say you do?
o: stand at the back wall and sing.
argue with the priests until they relent.
games.why: he sings from outside the west wall. tradition says the wall cracked and Krishna turned to face him.

practice: Picture yourself outside a wall, the way Kanaka stood: maybe a real place where you felt unwelcome, maybe just the sense that God, or meaning, is somewhere you can't see.
Sing inwardly, or just long, and picture a small window opening, and something on the other side turning toward you. If you pray, speak through that window; if not, stay by the wall, unhurried.

wordCard.voice: Kanakana kindi, Kanaka's window. A shepherd poet of Madhva's tradition kept outside the temple, and a Krishna who, the story says, turned to face him through it.

orig.note: Kannada: kanakana kindi, 'Kanaka's window' at the Udupi Krishna temple.

carryVoice: Your line: God turns toward the devotee left outside. Even a wall can become a window. Day two ninety-one.
